core_difference: Classification predicts categories, whereas regression predicts continuous numerical values.
when_left: Use classification when the target is a label such as pass/fail or defect type.
when_right: Use regression when the target is a quantity such as cycle time or concentration.
caveat: The same algorithm family may support both tasks, but metrics, output interpretation, and error costs differ.

core_difference: Precision measures correctness among predicted positives, whereas recall measures coverage among actual positives.
when_left: Emphasize precision when false alarms are expensive.
when_right: Emphasize recall when missing a true positive is expensive.
caveat: The classification threshold usually trades one metric against the other.

core_difference: Standardization centers and scales by standard deviation, while normalization rescales by a range or vector norm.
when_left: Use standardization for many linear, distance-based, and neural models when features have different units.
when_right: Use normalization when a bounded range or unit-length representation is required.
caveat: Both transformations must be fit using training data only.

core_difference: Overfitting captures training-specific noise, while underfitting fails to capture the main signal.
when_left: Address overfitting with simpler models, regularization, more representative data, or stronger validation.
when_right: Address underfitting with better features, more appropriate model capacity, or improved optimization.
caveat: A leakage-prone validation design can hide both problems.

core_difference: Bagging trains learners largely independently and averages them to reduce variance, while boosting trains learners sequentially to correct errors.
when_left: Use bagging when unstable base learners benefit from averaging.
when_right: Use boosting when incremental error correction can improve predictive accuracy.
caveat: Boosting can be more sensitive to noise and hyperparameters.

core_difference: Random forests average many randomized trees, while gradient boosting builds trees sequentially to improve the current ensemble.
when_left: Use random forests as robust nonlinear baselines with limited tuning.
when_right: Use gradient boosting when careful tuning and strong tabular performance are priorities.
caveat: Both require leakage-safe validation and subgroup error analysis.

core_difference: L1 encourages sparse coefficients and can set some to zero, while L2 smoothly shrinks coefficients.
when_left: Use L1 when sparsity and variable selection are desirable.
when_right: Use L2 when many correlated predictors may each contribute some signal.
caveat: Scale features before applying either penalty.

core_difference: MAE weights absolute errors linearly, while RMSE gives larger errors more influence through squaring.
when_left: Use MAE when a typical error in target units is easy to interpret.
when_right: Use RMSE when large errors deserve stronger penalties.
caveat: Review both with residual plots because neither reveals all error patterns.

core_difference: ROC-AUC summarizes ranking across true-positive and false-positive rates, while PR-AUC focuses on precision and recall for the positive class.
when_left: Use ROC-AUC for broad discrimination comparisons.
when_right: Use PR-AUC when the positive class is rare and positive-case performance is central.
caveat: PR-AUC changes with prevalence, and both are threshold-independent summaries rather than operating-point metrics.

core_difference: A fixed split uses one validation partition, while cross-validation rotates validation across multiple folds.
when_left: Use a fixed split for large datasets or time-ordered deployment simulations.
when_right: Use cross-validation when data are limited and repeated estimates improve stability.
caveat: The split strategy must respect groups, entities, and time in either approach.

core_difference: CNNs emphasize local patterns with shared filters, while Transformers use attention to combine information across positions.
when_left: Use CNNs for efficient local visual pattern extraction.
when_right: Use Transformers when long-range context or flexible token interactions are important.
caveat: Architecture choice depends on data size, compute, latency, and deployment conditions.

core_difference: An LSTM is a gated recurrent network designed to retain information over longer spans than a basic RNN.
when_left: Use a simple RNN for small sequence baselines when dependencies are short.
when_right: Use an LSTM when longer temporal dependencies matter.
caveat: Both are sequential and may be slower than Transformer-based alternatives.

core_difference: LoRA trains compact low-rank updates while keeping base weights frozen, whereas full fine-tuning updates most or all model parameters.
when_left: Use LoRA for lower memory, smaller artifacts, and multiple domain adapters.
when_right: Use full fine-tuning when abundant data and compute justify maximum adaptation capacity.
caveat: Neither method fixes weak or incorrect training data.

core_difference: Supervised learning uses labeled targets, while unsupervised learning discovers structure without target labels.
when_left: Use supervised learning for prediction when reliable labels exist.
when_right: Use unsupervised learning for exploration, segmentation, compression, or anomaly discovery.
caveat: Unsupervised patterns require domain validation and are not substitute labels.

core_difference: One-hot encoding gives each category an independent sparse indicator, while embeddings learn dense vectors that can capture similarity.
when_left: Use one-hot encoding for low-cardinality categories and transparent linear models.
when_right: Use embeddings for high-cardinality items or neural models where learned similarity is useful.
caveat: Embeddings require sufficient data and may encode unwanted bias.

core_difference: Batch inference scores many records on a schedule, while online inference returns predictions request by request with low latency.
when_left: Use batch inference for periodic reports and large offline workloads.
when_right: Use online inference when an application needs immediate responses.
caveat: Online systems require stronger latency, availability, and observability controls.

core_difference: Data drift changes the input distribution, while concept drift changes the relationship between inputs and outcomes.
when_left: Investigate data drift when feature distributions move.
when_right: Investigate concept drift when predictive performance declines despite similar inputs.
caveat: Confirmed concept drift usually requires labeled outcomes.

core_difference: Calibration asks whether probabilities match observed frequencies, while discrimination asks whether positives are ranked above negatives.
when_left: Prioritize calibration when probabilities drive resource or risk decisions.
when_right: Prioritize discrimination when ranking cases is the main goal.
caveat: A model can be strong on one property and weak on the other.

core_difference: Feature engineering creates new representations, while feature selection removes or retains existing predictors.
when_left: Use engineering when domain transformations can expose signal.
when_right: Use selection when redundancy, noise, or interpretability are concerns.
caveat: Both steps must occur inside the validation workflow.

core_difference: A generative model represents how data or outputs can be produced, while a discriminative model directly predicts targets or decision boundaries.
when_left: Use generative models for content generation, simulation, or modeling joint structure.
when_right: Use discriminative models for focused prediction tasks.
caveat: The distinction has several formal definitions, so the task and model family should be stated clearly.
